newsitem.title: SWEDEN: TENNIS-FERREIRA LEVELS SOUTH AFRICA IN DAVIS CUP.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-FERREIRA LEVELS SOUTH AFRICA IN DAVIS CUP.

text.p: South African number one Wayne Ferreira, nicknamed the "Swede killer" by local media, beat Jonas Bjorkman to draw his country level 1-1 with Sweden in a Davis Cup quarter-final on Friday.
Ferreira defeated Bjorkman 6-3 6-4 2-6 7-6 (7-3) by withstanding determined resistance in the third and fourth sets.
That squared the world group tie after Sweden had taken a 1-0 lead on Thomas Enqvist's victory over Grant Stafford 7-5 2-6 6-4 6-1.

Ferreira and Bjorkman were meeting for the sixth time and Ferreira, world-ranked 10th, has won every time. In 10 meetings with the three members of the Swedish squad he has won nine, losing only to Nicklas Kulti, to earn his nickname.
He has also beaten Enqvist twice and will face him again in what could be a crucial reverse singles match on Sunday.
Bjorkman and Kulti face David Adams and Ellis Ferreira in Saturday's doubles. The winners of the tie will face Italy or Spain in the semifinals in September.
Ferreira began confidently against Bjorkman after saying he was playing his best tennis for months and won a textbook first set after the only service break in the sixth game.
In the second set Ferreira broke Bjorkman's serve in the fifth game to lead 3-2 and again for 5-2 before Bjorkman broke him.
The Swede was changing his game and though he could not save the set, his more aggressive play earned him an easy run through the third set.
However Ferreira remained calm and fought back in the fourth. He lost two match points before winning the game on a 7-3 tie-break when Bjorkman hit the ball into the tramlines.
"I was playing extremely well in the first and second sets but he played exceptionally well in the third and fourth," Ferreira said.
"He was hitting the ball deep and hard and I really felt a lot of pressure on my serve.
"But when I lose my serve I still have to be composed and focused and realise I can catch him in the next game and I did that.
"I've played him a lot of times. This time was the best."
Enqvist won the first match by taking control against Stafford in the third set.
The lanky Swede, who won the title in Marseille this year, said he knew it would be a hard match.
"He's a different style from others because he is trying to come in on every serve and he tried to put pressure on me," Enqvist said. "I was on the defence all the time."

Stafford, ranked 69th, did well with his strong backhand and good placements in the first two sets, cheered from the sidelines by a group of 20 South African supporters painted in their national colours.
Ranked 282nd early in 1996, Stafford broke Enqvist's serve in the seventh game of the first set but the Swede broke back in the 10th and broke again in the 12th.
The second set went to the 25-year-old South African but the match turned Enqvist's way when he came back from two break points in the third game of the third set.
"I was struggling in the second set," Enqvist said. "But in the third and fourth sets I think I served much better than in the first two sets ... I found my rhythm again."
The tie is being played on a slow indoor rubber matting surface, the same used when Sweden beat Switzerland 4-1 in the first round in February.
South Africa beat Russia 3-1 to earn this tie against Sweden, who have won the Davis Cup five times - four in the last 13 years - against South Africa's once.
